item.title: Opening Up Delta Sharing with Arrow
item.description:
The Python Delta Sharing connector has long had powerful internals powered by Delta Kernel and Arrow, but the core user-facing experience typically ended up with a Pandas DataFrame.

That’s no longer the case.

The earlier Python interface

If you’ve used the connector before, this is the API you may remember:

read_with_pandas.py
import delta_sharing

profile_file = "/path/to/recipient.share"
client = delta_sharing.SharingClient(profile_file)

client.list_all_tables()

table_url = profile_file + "#share.schema.table"
df = delta_sharing.load_as_pandas(table_url)
1
Even after creating a SharingClient, the read API still wants a manually assembled table URL.
2
The public Python read path lands directly in Pandas.

There are a few pain points here:

  • even after creating a SharingClient, you still build the "<profile>#<share>.<schema>.<table>" string yourself
  • the public read path lands directly in Pandas
  • It’s difficult to handle tables that are larger than memory

Together, they made the interface feel more manual than it needed to be (especially if working with large datasets).

Escaping Pandas

The connector is powered by Delta Kernel behind the scenes, which is using efficient methods (Arrow) to fetch the data. But those efficient paths were not exposed publicly, which meant you still ended up back in Pandas.

Arrow is a language-independent columnar format, which makes it a good way to hand data from one engine to another, and tools like DuckDB and Polars can consume it directly. Having direct access to Arrow unlocks a lot of interoperability.

The connector already had most of the ingredients needed to expose Arrow. They just were not presented as a clean public API.

So if you really wanted to, you could reach into internal classes and wire it up yourself.

Expand the internal workaround example 
internal_arrow_workaround.py
import os
import tempfile
from json import dump, loads

import pyarrow as pa

import delta_kernel_rust_sharing_wrapper as dks
from delta_sharing.protocol import DeltaSharingProfile, Table
from delta_sharing.rest_client import DataSharingRestClient


def _write_snapshot(temp_dir, lines):
    log_dir = os.path.join(temp_dir, "_delta_log")
    os.makedirs(log_dir, exist_ok=True)

    with open(os.path.join(log_dir, "00000000000000000000.json"), "w") as f:
        dump({"protocol": loads(lines[0])["protocol"]["deltaProtocol"]}, f)
        f.write("\n")
        dump({"metaData": loads(lines[1])["metaData"]["deltaMetadata"]}, f)
        f.write("\n")
        for line in lines[2:]:
            dump(loads(line)["file"]["deltaSingleAction"], f)
            f.write("\n")

    return f"file:///{temp_dir}"


profile = DeltaSharingProfile.read_from_file("/path/to/recipient.share")
rest_client = DataSharingRestClient(profile)
rest_client.set_delta_format_header()

try:
    response = rest_client.list_files_in_table(
        Table(name="table", share="share", schema="schema"),
    )

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
        table_uri = _write_snapshot(temp_dir, response.lines)
        interface = dks.PythonInterface(table_uri)
        snapshot = dks.Table(table_uri).snapshot(interface)
        scan = dks.ScanBuilder(snapshot).build()
        arrow_table = pa.Table.from_batches(scan.execute(interface))
finally:
    rest_client.remove_delta_format_header()
1
Reconstruct just enough Delta log state locally for Delta Kernel to treat the shared snapshot like a Delta table.
2
Force the connector onto the Delta-format path.
3
Reconstruct a temporary Delta log snapshot locally.
4
Materialize the scan result as an Arrow table yourself.

This shows that, without much effort, we should be able to:

  • expose Arrow directly
  • stop requiring manual construction of the table URL

A better public interface

With the newer table and Arrow APIs in place, you no longer need to reach into internal classes just to get Arrow out of a shared table.

That is what the newer interface gives us:

table_handle_and_outputs.py
import delta_sharing

client = delta_sharing.SharingClient("/path/to/recipient.share")
table = client.table("share.schema.table")
snapshot = table.snapshot(limit=10000)

# Materialize the same snapshot in different formats.
pdf = snapshot.to_pandas()
arrow_table = snapshot.to_arrow()
reader = snapshot.to_record_batch_reader()
1
The read target is now a first-class table object rather than a string you build yourself.
2
Move from the table handle to an explicit snapshot.
3
Keep the old Pandas landing zone when Pandas is what you want.
4
Get an eager pyarrow.Table for flexible handoff.
5
Get a streaming Arrow reader for batch-native consumers.

You can now work with shared data through a table and snapshot object, and choose the output format that best matches what you want to do next.

In the diagram below, the red path is the earlier public interface and the blue path is the newer table interface, with snapshot and change data feed reads.

Start with the batch reader

The most interesting part of the new interface is to_record_batch_reader().

That gives you an Arrow RecordBatchReader, which is a streaming interface rather than a fully materialized table. In practice, that means the connector can hand batches straight to another engine.

That same shape is useful anywhere the next tool already understands Arrow streams or Arrow-native objects.

  • DuckDB
  • Polars
  • DataFusion
  • PyArrow
import duckdb

reader = snapshot.to_record_batch_reader()
result = duckdb.connect().from_arrow(reader).limit(10).df()

See DuckDB’s SQL on Arrow docs.

import polars as pl

reader = snapshot.to_record_batch_reader()
polars_df = pl.from_arrow(reader)

See Polars from_arrow.

from datafusion import SessionContext

ctx = SessionContext()
reader = snapshot.to_record_batch_reader()
df = ctx.from_arrow(reader)
result = df.to_pydict()

See DataFusion’s Python Arrow IO docs.

reader = snapshot.to_record_batch_reader()

for batch in reader:
    print(batch)

See PyArrow RecordBatchReader.

There is another nice side effect here as well: you can pull the data incrementally, and control how those batches are consumed. This is useful when the result is large and you want to process or write batches while maintaining a low memory footprint.

For example, you can buffer ten record batches at a time, then flush each group to a separate Parquet file:

snapshot_batches.py
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

batches_per_file = 10
batch_buffer = []
file_index = 0

with table.snapshot().to_record_batch_reader() as reader:
    for batch in reader:
        batch_buffer.append(batch)

        if len(batch_buffer) == batches_per_file:
            pq.write_table(
                pa.Table.from_batches(batch_buffer),
                f"snapshot-{file_index}.parquet",
            )
            batch_buffer.clear()
            file_index += 1

    if batch_buffer:
        pq.write_table(
            pa.Table.from_batches(batch_buffer),
            f"snapshot-{file_index}.parquet",
        )
1
Control how many batches are buffered per output file. Batch sizes can vary, so this is not a fixed row count or memory limit.
2
Write any batches left after the loop, even if the buffer is not full. An empty snapshot produces no files.
Note

Here, incremental means consuming a snapshot in batches, not reading changes over time. This reader does not watch for later commits.

Use table.changes(...) for the change data feed: insert, update, and delete events within a version or timestamp range. Both interfaces can return a batch reader; the difference is which rows they return.

If you do want an eager object instead, to_arrow() is still there as the convenience method for materializing a full pyarrow.Table.

A good mental model is:

  • to_record_batch_reader() is the most flexible primitive
  • to_arrow() is the eager, fully materialized variant

Less overhead means better performance

These benchmarks compare the earlier Pandas API with the newer snapshot outputs, then compare the memory needed to write the result incrementally or all at once. Each method reads 100 million rows, repeated ten times.

The percentage improvements can be smaller at lower data volumes and more pronounced at higher volumes, especially the memory savings from incremental reads.

Does it actually run faster?

Expand the runtime benchmark script 
runtime_benchmark.py
"""Compare full materialization of shared data as Pandas and Arrow tables."""

from pathlib import Path

import delta_sharing

from common import arguments, measure, run

METHODS = ("legacy_pandas", "snapshot_pandas", "snapshot_arrow")


def read(args):
    if args.worker == "legacy_pandas":
        result = delta_sharing.load_as_pandas(
            f"{args.profile}#{args.table}", limit=args.rows, version=args.version
        )
        return len(result)
    snapshot = delta_sharing.SharingClient(args.profile).table(args.table).snapshot(
        limit=args.rows, version=args.version
    )
    if args.worker == "snapshot_pandas":
        result = snapshot.to_pandas()
        return len(result)
    result = snapshot.to_arrow()
    return result.num_rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = arguments()
    if args.worker:
        measure(args, read)
    else:
        run(args, Path(__file__), METHODS)
Runtime benchmark results for 100 million NYC taxi rows, across ten repetitions per method. Lower is better.
Method Mean runtime (s) Min (s) Max (s)
load_as_pandas(...) 115.48 107.47 134.39
snapshot.to_pandas() 115.81 100.46 154.17
snapshot.to_arrow() 60.87 57.95 66.59 
runtimeMeasurements = (await FileAttachment("benchmarks/results/scale-100m-20261117/runtime.jsonl").text())
  .trim().split(/\r?\n/).map(line => JSON.parse(line))

writeMeasurements = (await FileAttachment("benchmarks/results/scale-100m-20261117/memory.jsonl").text())
  .trim().split(/\r?\n/).map(line => JSON.parse(line))

benchmarkLabels = ({
  legacy_pandas: "load_as_pandas(...)",
  snapshot_pandas: "snapshot.to_pandas()",
  snapshot_arrow: "snapshot.to_arrow()",
  incremental_write: "Incremental batches",
  eager_write: "Read all, then write"
})

benchmarkBoxplot = (samples, methods, metric, plotWidth) => {
  const chartWidth = Math.min(plotWidth, 760);
  const color = method => method === "legacy_pandas" ? "var(--benchmark-old)"
    : method === "snapshot_arrow" || method === "incremental_write"
    ? "var(--benchmark-good)" : "var(--benchmark-new)";
  const positions = {x: metric, y: "method"};
  const format = value => value.toLocaleString("en-US", {
    minimumFractionDigits: 2, maximumFractionDigits: 2
  });

  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: chartWidth,
    height: methods.length === 3 ? 260 : 220,
    marginLeft: chartWidth < 480 ? 144 : 164,
    marginRight: 20,
    marginTop: 20,
    marginBottom: 48,
    ariaLabel: `${metric === "peak_mib" ? "Peak memory" : "Runtime"} distributions across ten benchmark repetitions`,
    style: {background: "transparent", color: "inherit", fontFamily: "inherit", fontSize: "12px", overflow: "visible"},
    x: {
      label: metric === "peak_mib" ? "Peak process memory (MiB)" : "Runtime (seconds)",
      grid: true,
      nice: true,
      zero: metric === "peak_mib",
      ticks: Math.max(3, Math.floor((chartWidth - 164) / 70))
    },
    y: {label: null, domain: methods, tickFormat: method => benchmarkLabels[method], tickSize: 0, padding: 0.35},
    color: {domain: methods, range: methods.map(color)},
    marks: [
      // Draw all measured runs separately, without duplicating the box mark's outlier dots.
      Plot.boxX(samples, {...positions, fill: "method", stroke: "method", fillOpacity: 0.18,
        strokeWidth: 1.7, insetTop: 12, insetBottom: 12, r: 0}),
      ...Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => Plot.dot(
        samples.filter(sample => sample.repetition === i + 1),
        {...positions, fill: "method", stroke: "var(--bs-body-bg)", strokeWidth: 0.7,
          r: 3.5, dy: (i - 4.5) * 2.6}
      )),
      Plot.tip(samples, Plot.pointer({
        ...positions,
        title: sample => `${benchmarkLabels[sample.method]}\nRun ${sample.repetition} of 10\nRuntime: ${format(sample.seconds)} s\nPeak memory: ${format(sample.peak_mib)} MiB`,
        fill: "var(--reading-surface-raised)",
        stroke: "var(--reading-border)",
        fontSize: 12,
        lineWidth: 28
      }))
    ]
  });

  const codeLabels = methods.every(method => benchmarkLabels[method].includes("("));
  if (codeLabels) {
    const labels = chart.querySelectorAll('[aria-label="y-axis tick label"] text');
    labels.forEach(label => label.classList.add("benchmark-code-label"));
    // Measure attached SVG text so the code backgrounds also fit after resizing.
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      if (!chart.isConnected) return;
      labels.forEach(label => {
        const bounds = label.getBBox();
        const background = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "rect");
        background.setAttribute("class", "benchmark-code-background");
        background.setAttribute("transform", label.getAttribute("transform"));
        background.setAttribute("x", bounds.x - 3);
        background.setAttribute("y", bounds.y - 2);
        background.setAttribute("width", bounds.width + 6);
        background.setAttribute("height", bounds.height + 4);
        background.setAttribute("rx", 3);
        label.before(background);
      });
    });
  }
  return chart;
}
benchmarkBoxplot(runtimeMeasurements,
  ["legacy_pandas", "snapshot_pandas", "snapshot_arrow"], "seconds", width)

Direct Arrow materialization reduced mean runtime by ~47% relative to Pandas.

What happens when you stop reading results all at once?

Expand the peak memory benchmark script 
memory_benchmark.py
"""Compare peak process memory and runtime for two Parquet write patterns."""

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import delta_sharing
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

from common import arguments, measure, run

METHODS = ("incremental_write", "eager_write")


def write(args):
    snapshot = delta_sharing.SharingClient(args.profile).table(args.table).snapshot(
        limit=args.rows, version=args.version
    )
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
        path = Path(directory) / "result.parquet"
        if args.worker == "incremental_write":
            rows = 0
            with snapshot.to_record_batch_reader() as reader:
                with pq.ParquetWriter(path, reader.schema, compression="snappy") as writer:
                    for batch in reader:
                        writer.write_batch(batch)
                        rows += batch.num_rows
        else:
            result = snapshot.to_arrow()
            rows = result.num_rows
            pq.write_table(result, path, compression="snappy")
        assert pq.read_metadata(path).num_rows == rows
        return rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = arguments()
    if args.worker:
        measure(args, write)
    else:
        run(args, Path(__file__), METHODS)
Peak process memory and runtime for writing 100 million NYC taxi rows to Parquet, across ten repetitions per method. Lower is better; green marks the best values.
Method Runtime mean (s) Peak mean (MiB) Peak max (MiB)
Incremental write from snapshot.to_record_batch_reader() 100.31 2,286.30 2,360.44
Read all via snapshot.to_arrow() then write 100.97 14,529.71 14,604.52 
viewof writeMetric = Inputs.select(new Map([
  ["Peak memory (MiB)", "peak_mib"],
  ["Runtime (seconds)", "seconds"]
]), {label: "Measure", value: "peak_mib"})
benchmarkBoxplot(writeMeasurements,
  ["incremental_write", "eager_write"], writeMetric, width)

Incremental writes reduced mean peak memory by ~84% relative to reading the full Arrow table and writing afterwards. Both patterns averaged about 100 seconds.

The shared measurement helper and run instructions are in the appendix.

These runs used a fixture based on NYC taxi data:

  • dataset: nyctaxi_2019 (scaled to 100M rows)
  • rows per run: 100,000,000
  • repetitions: 10

Easier to use, easier to integrate

Overall, the new developments with the Delta Sharing connector are a win for interoperability, performance, and user experience.

You can start with a table, choose the representation that fits the next step, and hand data to Arrow-native tools and engines much more directly.

Sources

  • Delta Sharing repository README
  • Issue #860: object-based Python API proposal
  • PR #949: snapshot Arrow materializers
  • PR #992: Arrow materializers for table changes

Appendix

Expand the shared measurement helper 
common.py
"""Run each measurement in a fresh process, including native allocations."""

import argparse
import importlib.metadata
import json
import platform
import random
import resource
import shutil
import socket
import statistics
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlparse


def arguments():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--profile", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--table", default="delta_sharing.default.nyctaxi_2019")
    parser.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=10_000_000)
    parser.add_argument("--repeat", type=int, default=10)
    parser.add_argument("--version", type=int)
    parser.add_argument("--worker")
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--checkpoint-dir", type=Path)
    return parser.parse_args()


def measure(args, operation):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    rows = operation(args)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
    assert rows == args.rows, (rows, args.rows)
    peak = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
    peak_bytes = peak if sys.platform == "darwin" else peak * 1024
    print(json.dumps({"method": args.worker, "rows": rows,
                      "seconds": elapsed, "peak_mib": peak_bytes / 1024**2}))


def run(args, script, methods):
    import delta_sharing

    profile = json.loads(Path(args.profile).read_text())
    endpoint = urlparse(profile["endpoint"])
    socket.getaddrinfo(endpoint.hostname, endpoint.port or 443)
    if args.version is None:
        args.version = delta_sharing.SharingClient(args.profile).table(args.table).version()
    metadata = {
        "table": args.table, "rows": args.rows, "repetitions": args.repeat,
        "table_version": args.version, "python": platform.python_version(),
        "platform": platform.platform(),
        "packages": {name: importlib.metadata.version(name) for name in
                     ("delta-sharing", "pyarrow", "pandas", "duckdb",
                      "delta-kernel-rust-sharing-wrapper")},
    }
    args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.output.with_suffix(".metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2) + "\n")
    existing = [json.loads(line) for line in args.output.read_text().splitlines()] if args.output.exists() else []
    rng = random.Random(42)
    for repetition in range(args.repeat):
        order = list(methods)
        rng.shuffle(order)
        for method in order:
            if any(r["method"] == method and r["repetition"] == repetition + 1 for r in existing):
                continue
            command = [sys.executable, str(script), "--worker", method,
                       "--profile", args.profile, "--table", args.table,
                       "--rows", str(args.rows), "--version", str(args.version),
                       "--output", str(args.output)]
            result = subprocess.run(command, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=900)
            if result.returncode:
                raise RuntimeError(f"{method} failed: {result.stderr[-3000:]}")
            row = json.loads(result.stdout.strip().splitlines()[-1])
            row["repetition"] = repetition + 1
            with args.output.open("a") as output:
                output.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")
            existing.append(row)
            if args.checkpoint_dir:
                args.checkpoint_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                shutil.copyfile(args.output, args.checkpoint_dir / args.output.name)
            print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
    summary = []
    for method in methods:
        samples = [r for r in existing if r["method"] == method]
        seconds = [r["seconds"] for r in samples]
        peaks = [r["peak_mib"] for r in samples]
        summary.append({"method": method, "repetitions": len(samples),
                        "mean_seconds": statistics.mean(seconds),
                        "min_seconds": min(seconds), "max_seconds": max(seconds),
                        "peak_mean_mib": statistics.mean(peaks), "peak_max_mib": max(peaks)})
    args.output.with_suffix(".summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")

The benchmark scripts use the shared helper above.

  1. Download runtime_benchmark.py, memory_benchmark.py, and common.py into the same directory.
  2. Run each benchmark with your recipient profile and table name, using a separate output file:
python runtime_benchmark.py \
  --profile /path/to/recipient.share \
  --table share.schema.table \
  --rows 100000000 \
  --output runtime-results.jsonl

python memory_benchmark.py \
  --profile /path/to/recipient.share \
  --table share.schema.table \
  --rows 100000000 \
  --output memory-results.jsonl

Each measurement runs in a fresh process and checks the row count. Method order is shuffled; the results also record the table version and package versions.

This post was written with assistance from AI tooling.

item.title: Collecting large results with {sparklyr}
item.description:
NoteNotice

Originally published on Medium on June 24, 2023. The examples and benchmarks below are from the original post.

If you’ve ever wanted to take a large set of data from Spark back into the R session (or even Python) you’ll likely have experienced issues with performance, or been blocked completely by errors.

Example error:

Error : java.lang.OutOfMemoryError
... // and then the remainder of a large error

This error is the one I typically see people struggle with, sometimes trying inventive solutions that are tedious and/or error-prone.

The error happens when you’re hitting the 2GB limit that Spark sets. Without getting into the specifics of what can’t be changed on Spark side, I’ll show you how to collect() as much data as your R session will allow.

How to re-create the error reliably

I’ve got easy access to a Databricks environment, so I’ll be using that to create the dataset and run code.

We need a large enough dataset to play around with. The Spark SQL snippet below was run on Databricks and persisted to my schema within the metastore.

-- this looks a bit weird but it avoids exploding just once which is slower for a large array
create or replace table zacdav.collect_sample_data as
with tenmillion as (
  select
    round(rand() * 10000) as a,
    round(rand() * 10000) as b,
    round(rand() * 10000) as c,
    round(rand() * 10000) as d,
    round(rand() * 10000) as e,
    round(rand() * 10000) as f,
    round(rand() * 10000) as g,
    round(rand() * 10000) as h,
    round(rand() * 10000) as i,
    round(rand() * 10000) as j,
    round(rand() * 10000) as k
  from (explode(sequence(1, 10000000, 1)))
)
select * from tenmillion
union
select * from tenmillion
union
select * from tenmillion

A table of 30M rows x 11 columns of random numeric values should be enough.

Let’s try to collect this into the R session with {sparklyr}. We’re going to make sure that {arrow} is installed as it dramatically improves performance.

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

# oh what a surprise, this errors - we've got a reproducible example
results <- tbl(sc, "zacdav.collect_sample_data") %>%
  collect()

Success, the sample dataset reproduces the error.

Turns out if you were to spend time, like I did, collecting slightly less until the collect() executes successfully you’ll find that approximately 24 million rows is the maximum allowed (for this particular dataset, mileage will vary).

# turns out we hit the limit of `collect` at roughly 24 million rows
# this is a function of dataset number of columns, types of columns, etc
results <- tbl(sc, "zacdav.collect_sample_data") %>%
  head(24000000) %>%
  collect()

I don’t really want to have to slice my dataset into fractions manually and collect each part separately. So what now?

Understand how to circumvent the error

If we start looking under the covers of {sparklyr} we learn a few things:

  • When {arrow} is enabled, sdf_collect() calls arrow_collect(), a non-exported function.
  • arrow_collect() will accept a callback, and if specified will pull each batch incrementally (code).
  • If a callback isn’t specified then batch conversion happens all in one go (code).

The callback is particularly interesting, it’s exactly what we’re going to use to collect our large dataset. For those unfamiliar with callbacks, it’s essentially code that is invoked by other code - typically code that’s supplied as an argument to a function.

A callback is just an R function that will be called over each Spark partition

  • Chapter 8.4, Mastering Spark with R

The conditional block that is evaluated when specifying a callback invokes code that allows the Arrow batches to be pulled back iteratively rather than all at once (which is where we hit the error).

This solution isn’t completely new. Mastering Spark with R also describes using a callback to write each partition to disk or send it over the network, rather than collecting everything into memory.

Write a function to collect the whole dataset

Okay let’s write a function collect_larger() that directly calls arrow_collect() and specifies a callback that appends each batch to a list and combines it.

collect_larger <- function(tbl, ...) {
  collected <- list()
  sparklyr:::arrow_collect(tbl, ..., callback = function(batch_df) {
    collected <<- c(collected, list(batch_df))
  })
  data.table::rbindlist(collected)
}

It’s not the most elegant solution - ideally we wouldn’t need this at all. Nor is this the only solution: the callback’s behaviour could change depending on what you’re doing (e.g. you may want to persist each batch as a file to disk immediately).

If we try collect_larger() we can now collect the whole dataset!

# with new function we can collect whole dataset without issue
results <- tbl(sc, "zacdav.collect_sample_data") %>%
  collect_larger()

Benchmarking the solution

Problem solved! However, is performance comparable to using collect()?

I ran collect_larger() on the whole dataset prior to ensure caching. This ensures that I’m not measuring time spent scanning data.

# microbenchmark is great for this
library(microbenchmark)

dataset <- tbl(sc, "zacdav.collect_sample_data")

benchmark_results <- microbenchmark(
  collect_1m = head(dataset, 1000000) %>% collect(),
  collect_larger_1m = head(dataset, 1000000) %>% collect_larger(),
  collect_5m = head(dataset, 5000000) %>% collect(),
  collect_larger_5m = head(dataset, 5000000) %>% collect_larger(),
  collect_20m = head(dataset, 20000000) %>% collect(),
  collect_larger_20m = head(dataset, 20000000) %>% collect_larger(),
  times = 5
)
sparklyrBenchmark = await FileAttachment("benchmark-summary.json").json()
viewof sparklyrScale = Inputs.select(new Map([
  ["Logarithmic", "log"],
  ["Linear", "linear"]
]), {label: "Scale", value: "log"})
{
  const data = sparklyrBenchmark.results;
  const chartWidth = Math.min(width, 760);
  const format = value => value.toFixed(6);
  const position = {y: "case"};
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: chartWidth,
    height: 360,
    marginLeft: chartWidth < 480 ? 134 : 152,
    marginRight: 20,
    marginTop: 20,
    marginBottom: 44,
    ariaLabel: "Original benchmark runtime summaries: minimum, quartiles, median, maximum, and mean, in seconds.",
    style: {background: "transparent", color: "inherit", fontFamily: "inherit", fontSize: "12px", overflow: "visible"},
    x: {
      type: sparklyrScale,
      domain: [sparklyrScale === "log" ? Math.min(...data.map(d => d.min)) * 0.9 : 0,
        Math.max(...data.map(d => d.max)) * 1.1],
      ticks: sparklyrScale === "log" ? [3, 10, 30] : [0, 20, 40, 60],
      label: "Time [seconds]",
      grid: true
    },
    y: {label: null, domain: data.map(d => d.case).reverse(), tickSize: 0, padding: 0.3},
    color: {domain: ["collect()", "collect_larger()"],
      range: ["var(--benchmark-new)", "var(--benchmark-old)"], legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(data, {...position, x1: "min", x2: "max", stroke: "method", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      Plot.barX(data, {...position, x1: "q1", x2: "q3", fill: "method", fillOpacity: 0.22,
        insetTop: 10, insetBottom: 10}),
      Plot.tickX(data, {...position, x: "median", stroke: "method", strokeWidth: 1.8,
        insetTop: 10, insetBottom: 10}),
      Plot.dot(data, {...position, x: "mean", fill: "method", r: 3.5}),
      Plot.tip(data, Plot.pointerY({
        ...position, x: "mean",
        title: d => `${d.case}\nRows: ${d.rows.toLocaleString("en-US")}\nRepetitions: ${sparklyrBenchmark.repetitions}\nMean: ${format(d.mean)} s\nMedian: ${format(d.median)} s\nMin: ${format(d.min)} s\nQ1: ${format(d.q1)} s\nQ3: ${format(d.q3)} s\nMax: ${format(d.max)} s`,
        fill: "var(--reading-surface-raised)", stroke: "var(--reading-border)",
        fontSize: 11, lineWidth: 24
      }))
    ]
  });

  const labels = chart.querySelectorAll('[aria-label="y-axis tick label"] text');
  labels.forEach(label => label.classList.add("benchmark-code-label"));
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    if (!chart.isConnected) return;
    labels.forEach(label => {
      const bounds = label.getBBox();
      const background = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "rect");
      background.setAttribute("class", "benchmark-code-background");
      background.setAttribute("transform", label.getAttribute("transform"));
      background.setAttribute("x", bounds.x - 3);
      background.setAttribute("y", bounds.y - 2);
      background.setAttribute("width", bounds.width + 6);
      background.setAttribute("height", bounds.height + 4);
      background.setAttribute("rx", 3);
      label.before(background);
    });
  });
  return chart;
}

There is significant overhead for collecting data with collect_larger(), approximately ~35% for the 20 million row dataset - hardly surprising. This overhead is less (~25%) on the smaller dataset of 1 million rows.

I believe this overhead is worth it in order to be able to retrieve the entire dataset in one call - something that isn’t simple for larger datasets. It’s an easy solution that will let you focus on other things.

You can find the notebook to reproduce my results here.

Happy collect()-ing.

Noteworthy points

  • If you modify the callback to print out the size of each batch returned you’ll find almost always they are 10,000 rows. This is due to spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch, which defaults to 10,000.
  • There is certainly overhead for pulling back many small batches of 10,000 and combining those into a singular data.frame / data.table. You can test setting spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch to higher values to eke out extra performance if you’re inclined.
  • Consider if you could use a Spark UDF to run your analysis (or even convert code to {sparklyr}) as an alternative to collecting large data back to the driver node’s R session.
  • In collect_larger() I used {data.table}’s rbindlist() since I’ve found it to be faster in the past - unsure if that’s changed since I last benchmarked!
  • You’ll need to have sufficient memory available for the R session to collect() large data. My Databricks cluster had 128 GB of memory on the driver node, which is well above what is required to collect this amount of data.
